extracted.intended_audience: Practitioners and managers who practice before the USPTO (patent/trademark attorneys), counsel/respondents in USPTO OED disciplinary proceedings, and law-firm compliance officers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria governing practitioner conduct before the USPTO (esp. trademark signature rules, supervision, candor, communication, cooperation) and the factors used to determine violations and sanctions in OED disciplinary proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO authority to discipline (35 U.S.C. § 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director of the USPTO may suspend or exclude a person from practice before the Office if the person is 'shown to be incompetent or disreputable, or guilty of gross misconduct,' or if the person violates regulations established by the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary hearings require notice and opportunity for a hearing; proceedings conducted under USPTO procedural rules and 5 U.S.C. § 556 (impartial hearing officer). Case law upholds USPTO's exclusive authority to regulate practice before it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirement: notice and opportunity for hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must receive 'notice and opportunity for a hearing' before suspension or exclusion is imposed (35 U.S.C. § 32).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary hearings are conducted per 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.39, 11.44 and section 7 of the Administrative Procedure Act; Administrative Law Judges may be appointed to hear USPTO cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101 et seq.)
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO's Rules of Professional Conduct apply to persons who practice before the Office and are modeled on the ABA Model Rules to provide consistent standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rules govern duties such as diligence, communication, supervision, candor, and cooperation; decisions cite prior USPTO disciplinary precedents and ABA Standards when imposing sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof: clear and convincing evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence; a respondent bears the burden to prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear and convincing is an intermediate standard between preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt: evidence must produce firm belief or conviction. 'Clear' = certain/unambiguous; 'convincing' = reasonable and persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO trademark signature requirement (37 C.F.R. § 2.193(a); TMEP §611.01(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Signatures on trademark documents must be 'personally entered by the person named as the signatory.' A paralegal, legal assistant, or secretary may not sign the name of a qualified practitioner or other authorized signatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signature method used (DIRECT, ESIGN-ON, handwritten) matters: ESIGN-ON generates links for clients to sign; DIRECT means the preparer types signature between forward slashes (must be the signatory); filings include metadata (e.g., filing receipt IP address) that can show origin of submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature methods and evidentiary implications (DIRECT, ESIGN-ON, handwritten)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three methods to sign with TEAS: DIRECT (typed signature between slashes by the signatory), ESIGN-ON (TEAS-generated link sent to signatory who signs and returns), and handwritten (ink signature transmitted to filer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ESIGN-ON links were used there should be outgoing/incoming emails for each filing; absence of such emails may indicate improper signing. Filing receipts showing IP addresses may indicate submission origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of diligence (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are required to act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client; a diligent lawyer acts 'with commitment and dedication to the interests of the client.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What is 'reasonable' is context-dependent and measured against a reasonably prudent and competent practitioner. Delegation of ministerial tasks (like obtaining client signatures) is permitted only if the practitioner can reasonably ensure compliance with the law and rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deceit is behavior meant to fool; misrepresentation includes false or misleading assertions and conduct amounting to a false assertion. Violations generally require requisite intent (knowledge/intent), and absence of intent may distinguish negligence from deceit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not engage in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice, including conduct that impedes dispute resolution or frustrates fair balance essential to proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such misconduct can undermine public confidence in the legal system. In some jurisdictions/rulings, this misconduct may be established by negligence alone and does not always require intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to communicate with clients (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3), (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter and explain the matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonableness, not strict promptness, is the textual requirement; timeliness is a relevant factor in assessing reasonableness. Communications should be clear and provide sufficient context for informed decisions (vague or misleading client surveys may be inadequate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of candor to the USPTO (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a),(b),(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not knowingly fail to correct a false statement of material fact or law previously made to the USPTO and must take reasonable remedial measures if they know evidence offered is false; in ex parte proceedings practitioners must inform the Office of all material facts known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge (actual knowledge, inferable from circumstances) is essential to these rules. Remedial measures may include disclosure to the USPTO; mere suspicion without proof may affect whether disclosure is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervisory obligations for managers (37 C.F.R. § 11.501(a),(b),(c)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner with managerial authority must make reasonable efforts to ensure measures are in place reasonably assuring that the conduct of all practitioners in the firm conforms to the disciplinary rules; responsible for subordinate violations if the manager knows of the conduct when consequences can be avoided or mitigated but fails to take reasonable remedial action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable efforts may include hiring qualified supervisors, training, compliance procedures, audits, and remedial steps. Managerial authority does not automatically equal direct day-to-day supervisory responsibility—evidence of direct supervision is required to impose direct responsibility for a subordinate's misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligations regarding non-practitioner assistants (37 C.F.R. § 11.503(a),(b),(c)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must make reasonable efforts to ensure that non-practitioner assistants' conduct is compatible with the practitioner's professional obligations; practitioners with direct supervisory authority must make reasonable efforts to ensure non-practitioners conform to professional obligations and take remedial action when they know misconduct has occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures may include training, local manager oversight, written policies, and audits. Lack of direct supervisory control (e.g., remote foreign office managers) affects whether a practitioner is responsible for non-practitioner misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperation with OED investigations (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: In connection with a disciplinary matter, practitioners shall not fail to disclose a fact necessary to correct a known misapprehension, fail to cooperate with an OED investigation, or fail to respond to a lawful demand for information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses must not be misleading or evasive; correcting misunderstandings promptly (e.g., supplemental responses after an interview) mitigates misconduct allegations. Excuses about cost/time must not be phrased so as to mislead investigators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catchall misconduct provision (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibits 'other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be alleged and supported by evidence; claims not supported may be deemed waived. This is a broad backstop for conduct that does not fit other enumerated subsections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Before imposing sanctions, consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty to a client/public/legal system/profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused; and (4) existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary purpose of discipline is protection of the public and the bar, not punishment. Sanctions should be proportional to the violation; evaluators often consult ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions. Aggravating factors (e.g., pattern of misconduct) and mitigating factors (e.g., lack of prior discipline, remorse, remedial steps) influence severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental state distinctions for misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Different rules require different mental states: certain violations (e.g., deceit, misrepresentation) require intent/knowledge, while other misconduct (e.g., prejudicial conduct) may be established by negligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of whether conduct was negligent vs intentional affects both violation characterization and sanction severity. Negligence is defined as failure to take reasonable care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of supervisory responsibility (direct vs general authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Responsibility for others' misconduct hinges on whether the practitioner had direct supervisory authority (day-to-day control) versus general managerial authority; direct supervision obligations under §§ 11.501(b) and 11.503(b) require evidence of actual direct oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence such as who performed performance reviews, who made hiring/termination decisions, who provided direct training and audits, and frequency of interactions informs whether supervisory responsibility existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate remedial actions when misconduct is discovered
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasonable remedial measures include freezing filings, conducting investigations, providing additional training, requiring professional responsibility commitments, contacting affected clients, filing client ratifications with the USPTO, and hiring auditors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedial steps taken promptly and credibly can mitigate sanctions and may cure potential defects (e.g., filing client ratifications). The adequacy of remedial actions is judged in context (scope, timeliness, and effectiveness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of evidentiary metadata (filing receipts/IP addresses) to prove origin of filings
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO filing receipts include the IP address of the computer that made the submission and can be used to show filings originated from non-signatory locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of ESIGN-ON email records plus filing IP data may be strong circumstantial evidence that non-practitioner assistants entered signatures rather than clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for publication and appellate rights
rubrics_metrics.description: OED decisions may result in publication (e.g., notice in the USPTO Official Gazette) and parties have appeal rights (e.g., appeal to the USPTO Director within 30 days per 37 C.F.R. § 11.55(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication language should be materially consistent with the decision; appeal deadlines and procedures are strictly applied.
